concept.name: Standard error
concept.definition: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic - most commonly the standard error of the mean, which measures how much a sample mean would vary from sample to sample. It shrinks with the square root of the sample size.
concept.intuition: The standard deviation describes spread of individual data points; the standard error describes the spread of your estimate. It answers 'how precisely does my sample pin down the average?'
concept.mechanics: For the sample mean of n independent observations with population standard deviation sigma, the standard error is sigma/sqrt(n), estimated in practice by s/sqrt(n). Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error, and it is the denominator ingredient of t-statistics and confidence-interval widths.
concept.formula: SE(x_bar) = sigma / sqrt(n), where sigma is the population standard deviation and n the sample size; estimated as s / sqrt(n) from a sample.
concept.failure_modes: The sigma/sqrt(n) form assumes independent observations; with autocorrelated returns (volatility clustering, momentum), true standard errors are larger and naive intervals are too narrow. It also measures only sampling variability, not model or estimation bias.
concept.misconceptions: Standard error is not the standard deviation of the data and does not shrink the spread of individual returns as n grows - only the uncertainty of the mean. A small SE also does not validate the model; biased sampling yields precise but wrong estimates.
concept.example: Daily returns with sigma = 1.5% over n = 250 trading days give a standard error of the mean of 1.5%/sqrt(250) = 0.095%, so the estimated mean daily return carries about +/-0.19% (two SE) of sampling uncertainty.
